## Abstract {.unnumbered}

Your government decides how much to spend on each category the same way it has for decades: last year's number, plus whatever the loudest lobbyist got added, minus whatever the latest crisis forced a cut on. This is called "the budget process." It has no optimization function. It has no feedback loop. It has no measurable objective. It is, in the technical sense, not a process at all. It is an accident that repeats annually.

This specification describes the **Optimal Budget Generator (OBG)** framework, a systematic approach to generating integrated budget recommendations that maximize welfare as measured by two terminal general-welfare metrics: **real after-tax median income growth** and **median healthy life years**.

![Three ways to figure out optimal spending combine to show the gap between what you spend and what you should spend. The gap is filled with lobbyists.](/assets/images/optimal-budget-generator-spec/optimal-budget-generator-spec-section-abstract-unnumbered-bw-academic.jpg)

**JEL Classification**: H50, H61, D61, I18, C18

Unlike marginal-return frameworks that ask "where should we invest the next dollar?", OBG asks "what should the complete budget allocation be?" Each category has a target level - too little means underinvestment, too much means diminishing returns. But unlike the Recommended Daily Allowance for nutrients (where you can meet all targets simultaneously), every budget dollar has other uses: another category, a universal cash payment, or staying with the taxpayer who earned it. OBG generates integrated recommendations that compare all of these uses, so the total budget is an output of the model, not an input.

The framework combines three evidence sources: (1) **diminishing returns modeling** from dose-response studies, (2) **cost-effectiveness threshold analysis** from health economics, and (3) **reference-country spending data**, which enters the dose-response models as data but never sets a target by itself. The **Budget Impact Score (BIS)** measures our *confidence* in each category's OSL estimate based on the quality and quantity of causal evidence from the econometric literature.

The result is a gap analysis showing which categories are below evidence-based optimal levels, enabling systematic reallocation from overinvestment to underinvestment. Applied to the US federal budget, the illustrative example identifies pragmatic clinical trials as the most severely underinvested category (current spending is about 1% of the OSL, and the platform that runs these trials returns {{< var dfda_roi_rd_only >}}:1 in R&D cost savings alone), followed by basic research, early childhood education, and vaccinations.

**Scale note.** If budget allocation is the core bottleneck, the upside from fixing it is civilization-scale. Under the project's best-case governance ceiling, the recoverable upside is {{< var political_dysfunction_global_opportunity_cost_total >}} per year. Over 20 years, the [Optimal Governance Trajectory](../economics/gdp-trajectories.qmd) reaches {{< var wishonia_trajectory_gdp_vs_current_trajectory_multiplier_year_20 >}} the Earth baseline, raises average income to {{< var wishonia_trajectory_avg_income_year_20 >}} versus {{< var current_trajectory_avg_income_year_20 >}} on the status-quo path, and reaches {{< var wishonia_trajectory_gdp_year_20 >}} in total output. This specification focuses on the allocation layer of that plan; the full derivation lives in [The Political Dysfunction Tax](political-dysfunction-tax.qmd) [@political-dysfunction-tax-paper-2025].

Each OSL has a stated basis: a worked example in this paper (see [Worked Example: Pragmatic Clinical Trials](#worked-example-pragmatic-clinical-trials) and [Worked Example: Vaccinations](#worked-example-vaccinations)), the threat-based cost frontier for the military (see [Worked Example: Military Spending as a Cost Frontier](#worked-example-military-spending)), or the cash benchmark. Rows marked "Not derived" show only the direction of the evidence. OBG does not fill them with a multiple of current spending, because a target anchored on today's budget inherits today's errors.
:::

| Category | Current | OSL | Gap | Basis | Evidence | Income Effect | Health Effect | Action |
|----------|---------|-----|-----|-------|----------|---------------|---------------|--------|
| **Pragmatic clinical trials** | $0.5B | $50B | **+$49.5B** | Worked example | A (RCTs) | ++ | +++ | **Scale 100x** |
| Vaccinations | $8B | $16B | +$8B | Worked example | A (RCTs) | + | +++ | Increase |
| Military | {{< var us_military_spending_2024_annual >}} | {{< var us_defense_first_principles_optimal >}} | Cut {{< var us_gov_waste_military_overspend >}} | Threat-based cost frontier | C (assumption-based costs) | − | − | **Decrease** |
| Agricultural subsidies | $25B | $0B | -$25B | Cash benchmark | C (assumption) | − | − | Eliminate |
| Basic research | $45B | Not derived | Not derived | Evidence on direction only | Not graded | ++ | ++ | Estimate OSL; evidence says increase |
| Early childhood (0-5) | $50B | Not derived | Not derived | Evidence on direction only | Not graded | +++ | + | Estimate OSL; evidence says increase |
| Universal cash payment | $0 | Not estimated | Not estimated | Not estimated | | ++ | + | Estimate |

*Positive gaps indicate underinvestment; negative gaps indicate overinvestment. Income Effect: impact on real after-tax median income growth. Health Effect: impact on median healthy life years. Scale: +++ strong positive, ++ moderate positive, + weak positive, − negative. Evidence grades rate confidence in the OSL, not in the category's effects: early childhood programs have strong randomized evidence that more spending helps, but no estimate yet of the spending level where returns fall to the opportunity cost, so they have no OSL and no grade.*

The cuts in these rows are much larger than the increases. The OBG does not force the difference into any row. The full model assigns each dollar to its highest-value use: another category, a [universal cash payment](#universal-cash-payment-as-a-budget-category), or [lower taxes](#lower-taxes-as-the-final-benchmark). This example does not estimate those curves yet, so the difference stays unassigned.
